narrative:
The model estimated a 69.9% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. In practical terms, it judged failure more likely than success, and that risk estimate is why your law school application was denied.

The denial was driven mainly by your academic standing in law school. The strongest influence was your third-year class-rank band: you were in the lowest decile, while accepted students averaged around the sixth decile, and this factor pushed the prediction toward failure. The third-ranked factor was your first-year rank band, also the lowest decile versus an accepted average near the sixth decile, which independently added to the failure risk. Together, those two signals suggested a consistent pattern of low relative academic standing. Your LSAT score was the second most influential factor, and it worked in your favor, modestly pushing toward passing; at 37 it was only slightly below the accepted-student average of about 37.2. Even so, that positive signal was not enough to offset the academic-rank concerns.

To proceed, ask admissions for a human review or appeal, and submit any updated evidence that shows stronger academic performance or explains the low rank bands. Consider additional coursework or preparation that demonstrates readiness, and discuss with an advisor whether retaking the LSAT or seeking a provisional pathway would strengthen a future application.
